scenes.visual: Title card 'Shape Decides the Job' over two GOLD hexagon chains, one coiled, one straight. Same colour map as the first film. COLOUR MAP (both films): simple sugar = GOLD hexagon block; amino acid = BLUE round bead; nucleotide = GREEN bead with a small phosphate tab; fatty acid = ORANGE wavy tail; glycerol = ORANGE comb with three teeth; water = small LIGHT-BLUE bent 'V' labelled 'H2O'; links = short GREY bars between blocks. Two counters sit top right whenever links form or break: 'links' and 'waters'. All blocks are labelled cartoons, not molecular structures; every number appears only as on-screen text. Added for this film: digestive enzyme = BLUE folded blob with a notch-shaped pocket.

scenes.tts: Starch and cellulose are both chains of the same sugar, glucose. So why can your own enzymes take starch apart, but not cellulose?
scenes.visual: Two GOLD hexagon chains side by side, labelled 'starch' and 'cellulose'. Above both, a single GOLD hexagon labelled 'glucose' with an equals sign pointing to each. A question card: 'Why one and not the other?'
scenes.narration: Starch and cellulose are both chains of the same sugar, glucose. So why can your own enzymes take starch apart, but not cellulose?

scenes.tts: The first film showed food taken apart by adding water, one water per link. Here are the same gold sugar blocks. But their links are not all alike.
scenes.visual: Quick replay of the first film: a LIGHT-BLUE 'H2O' V snaps a GREY bar in a GOLD chain; counters tick. Then the two chains return; the GREY bars recolour by kind: starch's links along the chain one shade, its branch-point links a second shade, cellulose's links a third, labelled 'starch link', 'starch branch link' and 'cellulose link (schematic)'.
scenes.narration: The first film showed food taken apart by adding water, one water per link. Here are the same gold sugar blocks. But their links are not all alike.

scenes.tts: In starch, the glucose links let the chain coil, and some starch branches. It is the plant's store of sugar, and your enzymes can take it apart for energy.
scenes.visual: The starch chain curls into a spiral; a second starch chain beside it sprouts two side branches at branch-point links. Label 'starch: coils, and some branches (schematic)'. A small battery icon labelled 'energy store' appears beside it.
scenes.narration: In starch, the glucose links let the chain coil, and some starch branches. It is the plant's store of sugar, and your enzymes can take it apart for energy.

scenes.tts: A digestive enzyme is a protein folded into a pocket. Starch's links fit that pocket. The enzyme adds water at a link, and the chain breaks into smaller sugars. Other enzymes finish the job, down to glucose.
scenes.visual: A BLUE folded blob with a notch-shaped pocket slides along the starch spiral. When a GREY bar sits in the notch, a LIGHT-BLUE V enters and the bar snaps; short pieces of two or three GOLD hexagons drop off. A second, smaller BLUE blob then cuts those pieces into single hexagons labelled 'glucose'. Counters: links falling, waters used rising.
scenes.narration: A digestive enzyme is a protein folded into a pocket. Starch's links fit that pocket. The enzyme adds water at a link, and the chain breaks into smaller sugars. Other enzymes finish the job, down to glucose.

scenes.tts: In cellulose, the glucose blocks are linked the other way. The chains lie straight and stack side by side. Together they form strong fibers that stiffen plant cell walls.
scenes.visual: Straight GOLD chains slide in and stack in parallel rows, then bundle into a thick rope labelled 'fiber'. Zoom out: the ropes criss-cross inside a green rectangular plant cell wall, label 'plant cell wall'.
scenes.narration: In cellulose, the glucose blocks are linked the other way. The chains lie straight and stack side by side. Together they form strong fibers that stiffen plant cell walls.

scenes.tts: Now the same enzyme tries cellulose. Its pocket does not fit these links. Your own enzymes cannot break them. So for you, cellulose is fiber.
scenes.visual: The BLUE enzyme bumps against the straight cellulose chain; the notch and the link do not line up, a small red X flashes. No water enters; counters stay still.
scenes.narration: Now the same enzyme tries cellulose. Its pocket does not fit these links. Your own enzymes cannot break them. So for you, cellulose is fiber.

scenes.tts: Same sugar, different links, two shapes, two jobs. One stores energy; the other stiffens plant walls. The blocks, the links between them and the shape they take decide the job.
scenes.visual: Split screen: coiled starch with battery icon at left, straight cellulose rope in a plant wall at right. Text builds across the bottom: 'blocks + links + shape = job'.
scenes.narration: Same sugar, different links, two shapes, two jobs. One stores energy; the other stiffens plant walls. The blocks, the links between them and the shape they take decide the job.

scenes.tts: The enzyme follows the same rule. It is a protein, a chain of amino acids folded into a shape. That folded shape makes the pocket, and the pocket fits one kind of molecule.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the BLUE enzyme blob: it unrolls briefly into a chain of BLUE beads, label 'chain of amino acids', then refolds into the blob; the notch-shaped pocket glows. A GOLD starch link slides into the notch and fits; a GREEN bead and an ORANGE tail try and do not fit. Label 'pocket fits one kind of molecule'.
scenes.narration: The enzyme follows the same rule. It is a protein, a chain of amino acids folded into a shape. That folded shape makes the pocket, and the pocket fits one kind of molecule.

scenes.tts: Lipids follow the rule too. A phospholipid has a head that is attracted to water and two tails that avoid it.
scenes.visual: One phospholipid cartoon: a round ORANGE head with a small dark tab and two ORANGE wavy tails, labelled 'head: attracted to water' and 'tails: avoid water'. It bobs above a blue band of water.
scenes.narration: Lipids follow the rule too. A phospholipid has a head that is attracted to water and two tails that avoid it.

scenes.tts: Picture many phospholipids dropped into water, all tumbling at once. Each head likes water, and each pair of tails avoids it. Which way will the heads point?
scenes.visual: Dozens of phospholipid cartoons tumble into a blue water box, scattered at random angles. Question card: 'Heads point which way?'
scenes.narration: Picture many phospholipids dropped into water, all tumbling at once. Each head likes water, and each pair of tails avoids it. Which way will the heads point?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; a 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Out, toward the water, on both sides. The tails tuck into the middle. That double layer is the basic structure of a cell membrane.
scenes.visual: The phospholipids swing and settle into two rows: heads facing the water above and below, tails meeting in the middle. Label 'double layer: heads out, tails in'. The layer curves into a circle around a cartoon cell, label 'cell membrane'.
scenes.narration: Out, toward the water, on both sides. The tails tuck into the middle. That double layer is the basic structure of a cell membrane.

scenes.tts: Fats are lipids too, but a fat is not a chain. One glycerol holds three fatty acids by three links. Count from the free pieces, and three waters are missing. The water count still works. The chain picture does not.
scenes.visual: An ORANGE comb labelled 'glycerol' meets three ORANGE tails labelled 'fatty acid'. Each joins with a GREY bar and a dashed LIGHT-BLUE V drops into the tally box, labelled 'counted from free pieces'. Counters: links 0 to 3, waters 0 to 3. A 'chain?' tag is crossed out; label 'not a chain'.
scenes.narration: Fats are lipids too, but a fat is not a chain. One glycerol holds three fatty acids by three links. Count from the free pieces, and three waters are missing. The water count still works. The chain picture does not.

scenes.tts: Counting water only tells you how many links there are. It does not tell you the job. The blocks, the links between them and the shape they take decide what each molecule can do.
scenes.visual: Four panels in a row: coiled starch, cellulose fiber, the folded BLUE enzyme, the phospholipid double layer. Each gets a one-word job tag: 'store', 'support', 'cut', 'boundary'.
scenes.narration: Counting water only tells you how many links there are. It does not tell you the job. The blocks, the links between them and the shape they take decide what each molecule can do.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot. Take-home line: 'Blocks, links and shape decide the job.'
